beats.text: Leap years aren't every four years.
beats.visual_intent: frame 0: February calendar page with a cross

beats.text: The year of the seasons is about 365.24 days, so a leap day every 4 years overshoots.
beats.visual_intent: Earth on its orbit around the Sun, the 365.24 number, a quarter-day clock spilling over

beats.text: By the 1500s, the calendar had drifted about 10 days.
beats.visual_intent: calendar sliding away from a sun marker

beats.text: So in 1582, 10 days were skipped: October 4 was followed by October 15.
beats.visual_intent: October 1582 page, days 5 to 14 torn out

beats.text: And the rule changed: century years leap only if they divide by 400.
That's why 2000 had a leap day, and 2100 won't.
Every four years? Almost. Send this to someone born on February 29.

title_options: Leap years aren't every four years
publish.description: The year is about 365.24 days, so a leap day every four years overshoots. Since 1582, century years leap only if they divide by 400.

cta.decision_reason: February 29 birthdays are the people this rule affects most; sending it to one is a natural, specific share

beats.text: Skipping 3 century leap days every 400 years cancels the extra.
